concepts.name: Type erasure, generic `is` checks and unchecked casts

questions.prompt: `fun handle(payload: Any) { if (payload is List<String>) { /* ... */ } }` fails to compile. Why, and what is the usual fix?

choices.text: `is` needs a reified type, so marking `handle` as `inline` makes it legal
Type arguments are erased at runtime, so check `is List<*>` instead
`List` is an interface, so check against `ArrayList<String>` instead
`Any` blocks smart casts, so cast with `payload as List<String>` first

questions.explanation: Because of type erasure, Kotlin can't check at runtime which type arguments a generic instance was created with, so it refuses `is List<String>`. A star-projected check, `is List<*>`, is allowed, and its items are typed `Any?`. `inline` alone doesn't help: only a reified type parameter of an inline function can be checked, and `ArrayList<String>` is erased just the same.

sources.title: Generics: in, out, where
sources.claim: Due to type erasure there is no general way to check at runtime whether a generic instance was created with certain type arguments, so the compiler prohibits checks such as `is List<Int>`; checking against a star-projected type like `List<*>` is allowed, and only reified type parameters of inline functions can be checked.

questions.prompt: A Kotlin library module declares `class Cache { internal fun evictAll() { } }`. What does Java code in another module see in the compiled bytecode?

choices.text: Nothing, since `internal` compiles to package-private, which Java hides
A private method, plus a synthetic accessor that only Kotlin can call
A public method with a mangled name, so it is not used by accident
A public `evictAll()`, callable just like any other public method

questions.explanation: `internal` declarations become `public` in Java bytecode, but the compiler mangles the names of `internal` members. That prevents accidental overrides across modules (for example a Java subclass) and accidental use, though Java can still call the mangled name. Public members of an `internal` class are the exception: they are not mangled and stay callable from Java.

sources.title: Calling Kotlin from Java
sources.claim: `internal` declarations become `public` in Java; the compiler mangles the names of `internal` members to prevent accidental overrides across modules, while public members of `internal` classes aren't mangled and remain callable from Java.

questions.prompt: Your Hilt graph must supply `AuthRepository` (an interface, implemented by your `AuthRepositoryImpl` with an `@Inject` constructor) and a `Retrofit` instance. Which annotation do you use for each, and why?

model_answer.summary: Bind the interface to its implementation with an abstract `@Binds` function, and build `Retrofit` in a `@Provides` function, because you don't own it and it is created with a builder.
key_points: `@Binds` goes on an abstract function in an abstract module: its return type is the interface and its single parameter is the implementation, which must itself be injectable (an `@Inject` constructor)

`@Provides` is for types you don't own or that need a builder, like Retrofit, OkHttp or a Room database: the return type is what it provides, the parameters are its dependencies, and the body says how to build it
Prefer `@Binds` over a `@Provides` that just returns its parameter, because Dagger's generated code for `@Binds` is likely more efficient
Hilt runs an unscoped `@Provides` body every time it needs an instance, so an expensive object like Retrofit is usually scoped, for example with `@Singleton`

questions.explanation: Both annotations add a binding, but they say different things: `@Binds` only maps an interface to an implementation Dagger can already build, while `@Provides` contains code that builds an object Dagger can't construct itself. Writing every binding with `@Provides` works but adds code Dagger has to call.

sources.title: Dependency injection with Hilt
sources.claim: `@Binds` is an abstract function whose return type is the interface and whose parameter is the implementation to provide; `@Provides` supplies types you don't own or that use a builder (Retrofit, OkHttpClient, Room), where parameters are dependencies and Hilt executes the body every time it needs an instance.

sources.title: Binds (Dagger API)
sources.claim: `@Binds` methods must be abstract with a single parameter assignable to the return type, may be scoped, and are a drop-in replacement for `@Provides` methods that simply return an injected parameter; prefer `@Binds` because the generated implementation is likely more efficient.

questions.prompt: `readDictionary()` returns `Map<String, *>`. You write `val ints = readDictionary() as Map<String, Int>`, which compiles with an unchecked-cast warning. What happens at runtime if one value is really a `String`?

choices.text: The cast throws `ClassCastException` at once, as the values are checked
The compiler refuses the code, since unchecked generic casts are errors
Kotlin converts each value to an `Int`, failing only if it can't parse
The cast succeeds; the problem only shows up where a value is used

questions.explanation: A cast to a generic type with concrete type arguments can't be checked at runtime, because the arguments are erased: only the `Map` part is checked. So the cast succeeds, and the wrong value fails later, where code reads it as an `Int`. The compiler reports a warning, not an error, and casts never convert values.

sources.title: Generics: in, out, where
sources.claim: Type casts to generic types with concrete type arguments such as `foo as List<String>` cannot be checked at runtime; they are unchecked casts, reported with a warning, used when type safety is implied by program logic.

questions.prompt: A Kotlin SDK module marks its implementation classes and helper functions `internal`. A Java app uses the SDK. How do those declarations look to the Java code, and what should the SDK author keep in mind?

model_answer.summary: In bytecode `internal` becomes `public`, with mangled names for `internal` members, so Java can technically reach them; the author shouldn't treat `internal` as a hard barrier for Java callers.
key_points: `internal` has no Java equivalent, so `internal` declarations compile to `public` in the bytecode
The compiler mangles the names of `internal` members, which prevents accidental overrides across modules (such as a Java subclass) and makes accidental calls unlikely
Public members of an `internal` class are not mangled, so they remain callable from Java
So Java callers can still reach `internal` code; the module boundary is only enforced by the Kotlin compiler

questions.explanation: Module visibility is a Kotlin concept the JVM doesn't have. The mangling discourages Java use, but it is not access control, which matters when a library is used from Java.

sources.title: Calling Kotlin from Java
sources.claim: `internal` declarations become `public` in Java; the Kotlin compiler mangles the names of `internal` members to prevent accidental overrides across modules, and the names of public members of `internal` classes aren't mangled and remain callable from Java.

questions.prompt: A Hilt module has `@Provides fun repo(impl: AuthRepositoryImpl): AuthRepository = impl`, and `AuthRepositoryImpl` has an `@Inject` constructor. What does Dagger's documentation recommend?

choices.text: Replace it with an abstract `@Binds` method, likely more efficient
Keep it, as a `@Provides` that returns its parameter is how interfaces bind
Add `@Singleton` to it, because a binding for an interface must be scoped
Call `AuthRepositoryImpl()` in the body, so Dagger skips its constructor

questions.explanation: A `@Provides` method that only returns its injected parameter is exactly what `@Binds` replaces: an abstract method with one parameter assignable to the return type. Dagger says to prefer `@Binds` because its generated implementation is likely more efficient. Scoping is optional for both, and constructing the class by hand would bypass the injection of its own dependencies.

sources.title: Binds (Dagger API)
sources.claim: `@Binds` methods are a drop-in replacement for `@Provides` methods that simply return an injected parameter; prefer `@Binds` because the generated implementation is likely more efficient, and `@Binds` methods may be scoped.

questions.prompt: Your Hilt graph must supply `AuthRepository` (an interface implemented by `AuthRepositoryImpl`, which has an `@Inject` constructor) and a `Retrofit` instance. Which statements are right? Select all that apply.

choices.text: Bind `AuthRepository` with an abstract `@Binds` function in an abstract module
A `@Binds` function's body calls `AuthRepositoryImpl()` to build the instance
Create `Retrofit` in a `@Provides` function that uses its builder
Hilt runs an unscoped `@Provides` body only once and then reuses its result
Prefer `@Binds` to a `@Provides` that just returns its parameter

questions.explanation: `@Binds` goes on an abstract function in an abstract module: its return type is the interface and its single parameter the injectable implementation, so it has no body to call a constructor in. `@Provides` suits types you don't own or that need a builder, like Retrofit. Dagger recommends `@Binds` over a `@Provides` that only returns an injected parameter, because its generated code is likely more efficient. Hilt runs an unscoped `@Provides` body every time it needs an instance, which is why Retrofit is usually scoped, for example with `@Singleton`.

sources.title: Dependency injection with Hilt
sources.claim: `@Binds` is an abstract function in an abstract module whose return type is the interface and whose parameter is the implementation; `@Provides` supplies types you don't own or that need a builder (Retrofit, OkHttpClient, Room), and Hilt executes its body every time it needs an instance.

sources.title: Binds (Dagger API)
sources.claim: `@Binds` methods must be abstract with a single parameter assignable to the return type, and are a drop-in replacement for `@Provides` methods that simply return an injected parameter; prefer `@Binds` because the generated implementation is likely more efficient.

questions.prompt: A Kotlin SDK marks its implementation classes and helper functions `internal`, and a Java app uses the SDK. Which statements are true? Select all that apply.

choices.text: `internal` declarations compile to `public` in the Java bytecode
`internal` declarations compile to package-private, hiding them from Java
The compiler mangles the names of `internal` members in the bytecode
Java callers can't reach `internal` code, since the JVM enforces modules
Public members of an `internal` class keep their names, callable from Java

questions.explanation: `internal` has no Java equivalent, so `internal` declarations become `public` in Java, not package-private. The compiler mangles the names of `internal` members, which prevents accidental overrides across modules (such as a Java subclass) and makes accidental calls unlikely, but public members of an `internal` class aren't mangled and stay callable from Java. So Java code can still reach `internal` code: only the Kotlin compiler enforces the module boundary.

sources.title: Calling Kotlin from Java
sources.claim: `internal` declarations become `public` in Java; the Kotlin compiler mangles the names of `internal` members in bytecode to prevent accidental overrides across modules, and the names of public members of `internal` classes aren't mangled and remain callable from Java.
